{{Short description|Theorem in geometric topology}}
In [[geometric topology]],  the '''double suspension theorem''' of [[James W. Cannon]] ({{harvtxt|Cannon|1979}}) and Robert D. Edwards states that the double [[suspension (topology)|suspension]] ''S''<sup>2</sup>''X'' of a [[homology sphere]] ''X'' is a topological sphere.<ref>Robert D. Edwards, "[https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0610573 Suspensions of homology spheres]" (2006) ArXiv (''reprint of private, unpublished manuscripts from the 1970's'')</ref><ref>Robert D. Edwards, "The topology of manifolds and cell-like maps", ''Proceedings of the International Congress of Mathematicians'', Helsinki, 1978 ed. O. Lehto, Acad. Sci. Fenn (1980) pp 111-127.</ref><ref>James W. Cannon, "Σ<sup>2</sup> H<sup>3</sup> = S<sup>5</sup> / G", ''Rocky Mountain J. Math.'' (1978) '''8''', pp. 527-532.</ref>

If ''X'' is a [[piecewise-linear manifold|piecewise-linear]] homology sphere but not a sphere, then its double suspension ''S''<sup>2</sup>''X'' (with a triangulation derived by applying the double suspension operation to a triangulation of ''X'') is an example of a triangulation of a topological sphere that is not piecewise-linear. The reason is that, unlike in piecewise-linear manifolds, the link of one of the suspension points is not a sphere.
